la:verb:dido.gloss: to give out, spread abroad, disseminate, distribute, scatter
senses: to give out, spread abroad, disseminate, distribute, scatter
la:verb:dido.html:
dī-do (also written disdo;
v.the foll.), didĭdi, didĭtum, 3, v. a., to give out, spread abroad, disseminate, distribute (anteclass. and poet.; esp. in Lucr.; once in Tac.).
Lit.: numquam ego argentum ... disdidi, Cato ap. : in venas cibum,; ; ; cf. ; : omne per caules palati,; cf. ; ; .—Absol.: dide, disice, Caecil. ap. (Com. Frag. v. 239 Rib.).—
Trop.: dum munia didit (sc. servis),: per magnas didita gentes Solatia vitae,; cf.: rumor per agmina Trojana,: tua terris didita fama,; cf.: fama in populos,: fama per provincias,.

la:verb:diduco.gloss: to lead or draw apart; part, split, separate, sever, sunder, divide, loosen, open out
senses: to lead or draw apart; part, split, separate, sever, sunder, divide, loosen, open out
to separate, divide, distribute, deploy; disperse, scatter
la:verb:diduco.html:
dī-dūco, xi, ctum, 3,
v. a., to draw apart; to part, split, separate, sever, sunder, divide (class.).
Lit.
In gen.: ventus eas (sc. nubes) leviter diducit,: cum compresserat digitos pugnumque fecerat ... cum autem diduxerat et manum dilataverat, etc.,; of the graceful movements of the arms in dancing: molli diducit candida gestu brachia, (Müll. al. deducit): candida seu molli diducit brachia motu,; cf. oculum,: supercilium volnere diductum,: pedem et crus in diversa,: os,: nares, Quint 11, 3, 80: labra,: fauces immani hiatu,to stretch,: rictum risu, et saep.: nodos manu,; cf.: complexus vestros,: humum,; cf.: arva et urbes,: terram,: scopulos (Hannibal),; cf. of natural cleavings of the earth,; : cibum, i. e. to digest = digerere, ; v.the foll.: mixti neque inter se diducti colores, et saep.—With in: crudam materiam in corpus omne diduci, Cels. praef.: maxima flumina in rivos diducuntur,; cf.: domum in multos diductam recessus,. —
In partic. milit. t. t., to separate the forces, in a good or (more freq.) in a bad sense; to divide, distribute; to disperse, scatter: diductis nostris paullatim navibus,: instruunt aciem diductam in cornua, Drak.; cf.: diducta propere in cornua levis armatura est,: diductis in latera viribus, Oud.: ordines,; 2, 6, 4: copias,: cornua,: robur, Cort.; and poet.: choros,: ubi Crassus animadvertit, suas copias propter exiguitatem non facile diduci,; ; . 40, 2; ; ; ; ; et saep.—
Trop. (mostly post-Aug.): cum diducaris ab eo, quicum libentissime vixeris,; cf.: amicitias cohaerentes, Sen. de Ira, 2, 29: nuptias,; cf. matrimonium,; and: si repudio diducta fuerit,: diducta civitas ut civili bello,divided into parties,; cf. below: in sterili jejunaque materia, eandem speciem laudis diducere ac spargere,; cf. argumenta,; : nomina, Spald.: litem domini et conductoris,i. e. to settle, adjust, et saep.—With in: assem in partes centum,: in tres partes medicina diducta est, Cels. praef.: haec omnia rursus in species,; cf. ; : divisionem in digitos,to tell off on one's fingers, (coupled with partiri); cf. argumenta,: animum in tam multiplex officium,: ultio senatum in studia diduxerat,; ; cf.: seditio in diversa consilia diduxerat vulgum,; of classification, to divide: in tres partes medicinam, Cels. praef.

la:noun:Dido.html:
Dīdō, ūs and ōnis, f., Διδώ,
the celebrated foundress of Carthage, daughter of the Tyrian king Belus, wife of Sichaeus, and sister of Pygmalion; called also Elisa or Elissa.—Nom. Dido, ; ; et saep.; ; ; .—Gen. Dīdōnis, ; ; : Dīdūs, Cornutus ap. P.—Dat. Dīdō, (dub. al. Didoni): Dīdōni,.—Acc. Dīdō, ; ; (in both passages several MSS. read Didon); : Didonem,; : Dīdūn, Atteius ap. Charis. l. l.—Abl. Dīdōne, Enn. ap. P.; (cf. Neue Formenl. 1, 352).

la:adj:Didius.gloss: of or pertaining to the gens Didia.
senses: of or pertaining to the gens Didia.
la:adj:Didius.html:
Dīdĭus, a, um,
the name of a Roman plebeian gens; so T. Didius, consul in the year 656 a. u. c., ; ; Didius Julianus, emperor of Rome in the year 193 A. D., whose life is written by Spartianus.—
Adj.: Lex Didia sumptuaria, of the year 610 a. u. c.,. Another law: Lex Caecilia Didia, of the year 656,;
